primary_meaning: Reverent awe of God—recognition of his holiness, majesty, authority, and accountability before him—which produces humble worship, trust, rejection of evil, and obedient living. Christian teaching commonly distinguishes this from mere panic or servile terror, while allowing a genuine awareness of divine judgment.
primary_basis: Proverbs 1:7 — “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge.”
Proverbs 9:10 — “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom.”
Job 28:28 — fearing the Lord is identified with wisdom and turning from evil with understanding.
Psalm 111:10 — the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom and is associated with obedience.
Deuteronomy 10:12–13 — fearing God is joined with walking in his ways, loving, serving, and keeping his commandments.
Ecclesiastes 12:13 — fearing God is paired with keeping his commandments.
Proverbs 8:13 and 16:6 — fearing the LORD entails hatred of evil and turning away from it.
Isaiah 11:2–3 — delight in the fear of the LORD is associated with the Spirit resting upon the messianic king.
Acts 9:31 — the church walks in the fear of the Lord and the comfort of the Holy Spirit.

alternatives.meaning: Actual dread of divine punishment or judgment. On this reading, fear includes—or in some contexts primarily denotes—being afraid because God can judge and destroy.
basis: Exodus 20:18–20 — distinguishes immediate terror from the enduring fear intended to restrain sin.
Luke 12:4–5 — Jesus commands fear of the one who has authority to cast into hell.
Hebrews 10:31 — “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.”
Revelation 14:7 — fear of God is commanded in the setting of judgment.

alternatives.meaning: A comprehensive designation for covenant faithfulness or practical piety, rather than primarily an inward emotion. “Those who fear the LORD” thus means God’s faithful worshipers, characterized by allegiance, obedience, and right conduct.
basis: Deuteronomy 6:2 and 10:12–13 — fear encompasses obedience, love, service, and covenant keeping.
Psalm 25:12–14 and 103:11–18 — those who fear God are portrayed as covenant recipients who keep his commands.
Malachi 3:16–18 — those who fear the LORD are his remembered and treasured people.
Acts 10:2, 22, 35 — “God-fearer” language describes devout worshipers whose conduct accords with reverence for God.

alternatives.meaning: Filial fear: a childlike fear of offending, grieving, or being separated from God, contrasted with servile fear motivated chiefly by punishment. This is especially developed in Catholic and other classical theological traditions.
basis: Psalm 130:4 — forgiveness leads to fear or reverence rather than eliminating it.
Romans 8:15 — believers have not received a spirit of slavery leading back into fear but the Spirit of adoption.
2 Corinthians 7:1 — holiness is brought to completion in the fear of God.
1 John 4:18 — perfect love casts out fear associated with punishment.

alternatives.meaning: A distinct gift or disposition imparted by the Holy Spirit, traditionally numbered among the seven gifts of the Spirit and understood as profound reverence and unwillingness to offend God.
basis: Isaiah 11:2–3 — the Spirit of knowledge and the fear of the LORD rests upon the messianic figure, who delights in that fear.
Traditional Christian interpretation of Isaiah 11, especially in Catholic theology, applies the Spirit’s gifts to believers through participation in Christ.

notes: There is broad Christian consensus on reverent, obedient awe as the phrase’s primary teaching meaning, especially in wisdom and discipleship contexts. The expression is nevertheless context-sensitive: some passages emphasize real dread of judgment, while others use it as shorthand for covenant piety. Thus the consensus is settled at the broad level but does not reduce every occurrence to a single emotional sense.
